# Aspect Oriented Programming

A cross-cutting concern — logging, timing, auditing, usage counting — is one that would otherwise be
copy-pasted into every method that needs it. AOP moves it out of the methods and into an **aspect**:
a declaration of *where* (a pointcut) and *when* (an advice type) the extra behaviour runs. The
business code never mentions it.

Realised in `Information-Systems-Modelling` lab 4 on top of `spring-boot-starter-aop`. Four aspects
ship, and between them they exercise every advice type Spring AOP offers.

## The four aspects and what each demonstrates

| Aspect | Advice types | Pointcut | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `LoggingAspect` | `@Before`, `@AfterReturning`, `@AfterThrowing` | `execution(public * …service.*Impl.*(..))` | service-layer entry/exit/exception log |
| `PerformanceAspect` | `@Around` | `@annotation(…Timed)` | warn above a 500 ms threshold |
| `SecurityAuditAspect` | `@AfterReturning`, `@After` | one controller method, plus all admin calls | login-success/failure audit trail |
| `StatisticsAspect` | `@AfterReturning` | all controller methods **minus three** | endpoint call counting |

Two design details are worth more than the list:

**Pointcuts are written to exclude, not just to include.** `StatisticsAspect` targets every public
method in the `api` package and then subtracts `StatisticsController`, `AnalyticsController` and
`SystemController` with `!within(...)` — otherwise reading the statistics would increment them.
`LoggingAspect` targets only `*Impl` classes, which keeps analytics and controllers out of scope.
Both are the same instinct: an aspect that fires on itself is the classic AOP failure mode.

**`@Timed` is opt-in, not blanket.** Rather than time everything, a custom annotation marks the two
heavy JDBC aggregation methods (`AnalyticsService.dashboard()` and `.ai()`), and `PerformanceAspect`
binds its `@Around` advice to the annotation. Blanket timing would drown the signal.

## The rationale is recorded in the source

Unusually for this corpus, the *why* is written down rather than inferred:

> "Why AOP here instead of code in the controller: Controllers implement generated OpenAPI
> interfaces; adding audit calls inside them couples business logic to observability."
> — Information-Systems-Modelling/lab4/.../aspect/SecurityAuditAspect.java, 2026-05-28

That reason is specific to this codebase and follows directly from
[[contract-first-api-design]]: the controllers are implementations of *generated* interfaces, so
anything hand-added to them is at risk every time the generator runs. AOP puts the observability
somewhere the generator cannot reach.

## Where it sits in the stack

The aspects wrap the `api → service → repository → entity` split described in
[[layered-architecture]], which is what makes the pointcut expressions short: the package names
*are* the layers. Lab 4 is the only lab that uses AOP — labs 2 and 3 are its ancestors under
[[forward-copy-lab-progression]] and carry no `spring-boot-starter-aop` dependency.

## What is not verified

**Zero tests cover any of the four aspects.** Lab 4's entire Java test suite is one
`contextLoads()` and one `BuildsControllerIntegrationTest` with a single `@Test`. A pointcut that
silently stops matching — a renamed package, a controller that no longer ends in `Impl` — would fail
open and nothing would catch it.
